name: Mycenaean Greek
confidence_why: Linear B has no accent notation, so the Mycenaean word accent is simply unattested: Melena 2014 says so directly, García Ramón 2011 and Bernabé and Luján 2006 say the texts give no evidence about the accent, and the reference grammars of Bartoněk 2003, Risch and Hajnal 2006 and Lejeune 1972 have no accent section for Mycenaean, so no source disagrees.
catalog_citation: Melena, José L. 2014. 'Mycenaean writing', ch. 17 (pp. 1-186) in Y. Duhoux & A. Morpurgo Davies (eds.), A Companion to Linear B: Mycenaean Greek Texts and their World, vol. 3 (BCILL 133). Louvain-la-Neuve / Walpole MA: Peeters.
catalog_locator: §17.2.3, p. 15 (PDF page 22 of the archive.org scan; page image. scanned text); restated in the glossary §17.5, p. 171 s.v. word (PDF page 178; page image…
catalog_quote: There is no diacritic for ACCENT, but a kind of interpunction (usually known as ‘word divider’) often separates accentual units, which may consist of either a single word or a word group with only one main accent (i.e. an accented element together with proclitic or enclitic elements). [p. 171, s.v. WORD:] classical Greek inscriptions do not distinguish words and do not mark the accents. Linear B does not mark the accent either but uses the so called word divider, a small vertical bar, to separate sequences of signs. These may correspond to a single word (e.g. i-qo ‘horse’) or to a series of unaccented items and one accented form, here in bold (da-mo-de-mi /dāmos de min/ ‘people but her’; o-u-di-do-si /ou didonsi/ ‘not they-give’). In general the word divider marks an accentual unit, i.e. a phonological word, rather than a grammatical word or a semantic unit.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under ( present and accurate). (1) Quote: lines 957-960 read exactly 'There is no diacritic for ACCENT, but a kind of interpunction (usually known as 'word divider') often separates accentual units, which may consist of either a single word or a word group with only one main accent (i.e. an accented element together with proclitic or enclitic elements).' under the running head 'S17.2.3 MYCENAEAN WRITING 15'; lines 11479-11486 (glossary s.v. word, p. 171) read 'classical Greek inscriptions do not distinguish words and do not mark the accents. Linear B does not mark the accent either but uses the so called word divider.. In general the word divider marks an accentual unit, i.e.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated or recoverable: the Linear B syllabary has no means of marking accent, so the position of the Mycenaean word accent is unknown; the only accent-related fact the script yields is that clitics (o-u-, -qe, -de..) are written together with their host, i.e. the 'word' of the script is an accentual unit. Concordant first-hand statements: García Ramón 2011: 223 n. 21 'obviously Mycenaean does not provide any evidence about the accent'; Bernabé & Luján 2006: III (accents printed by Attic rules 'aunque no nos conste que fueran las mismas que en época micénica') and 142 ('algo sobre lo que los textos micénicos no nos ofrecen ninguna información').
new_statements.exceptions: None as such. Indirect inference only: Risch & Hajnal 2006 sect. 37e n. 182 / sect. 65 (after Klingenschmitt 1972) explain Myc. /or/ vs /ro/ < *r̥ by the position of the inherited accent, explicitly 'das griech. Dreisilbengesetz vorausgesetzt' -- i.e. they presuppose, but do not demonstrate, that the later Greek limitation/recessive system already.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns what the writing system records (word-level accent not notated; word divider delimits phonological word = host + clitics). Any accents seen on Mycenaean transcriptions in handbooks are the first-millennium Attic system applied by editorial convention (Bernabé & Luján 2006: III; García Ramón 2011: 223 n. 21).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements quoted describe Mycenaean Greek proper, i.e. the language of the Linear B tablets (Knossos, Pylos, Thebes, Mycenae etc., c. 1400-1200 BCE; ISO 639-3 gmy). Glottolog's languoid myce1241 is labelled 'Achaean Greek' and its bibliography mixes Mycenaean handbooks (Bartonek 2003, Ventris & Chadwick 1973, Doria 1965) with first-millennium Arcadian (Dubois 1986) and Cypriot (Egetmeyer 2010) grammars; nothing here concerns Arcadian or Cypriot. The language is extinct and attested only in a syllabic script that has no accent notation, so no first-hand placement rule can exist; any accentuation printed on Mycenaean transcriptions (e.g. Ruijgh, Bernabe & Lujan, Risch & Hajnal) is by explicit convention the Attic/first-millennium system projected back.
